question.text: A Cat III AIF creates a SIDE-POCKET when:

answer.text: It wants to reduce management-fee expense

A specific asset becomes illiquid, stressed, or materially hard-to-value, and the manager segregates it so that NAV of the rest of the fund remains tradeable and fair to subscribing/redeeming investors
The fund wants to bypass the 2x leverage cap
The manager wishes to concentrate all profitable trades

explanation.text: The Logic: Side-pocketing is used when a specific asset becomes illiquid, stressed, or materially hard to value. By segregating that asset into a separate sub-scheme, the manager protects the main scheme's NAV from mark-to-model uncertainty on the troubled holding, prevents new subscribers from inheriting stress they did not underwrite, and stops exiting investors from leaving at arbitrary marks. It is a fairness/valuation tool, not a fee or leverage technique. The Trap: Options A (management-fee reduction), C (bypassing leverage cap) and D (concentrating profitable trades) are fabricated motivations that misuse the segregation concept. Note: The specific claim that SEBI permits Category III AIFs to side-pocket stressed assets and the fairness mechanics described above are not explicitly set out in the cited XIX-E (Category III AIF Managers) workbook pages, which support redemption/valuation concepts generally. The framing reflects general industry/regulatory practice on handling illiquid assets within pooled vehicles.
